data.text/markdown:
Pooling: one model for all stocks, or one model per stock?

One question only: on the same stocks, days and inputs, does a model learned on one stock tell that stock's days apart better than one model learned on all stocks? No calls, no profit, no luck bars: the three ways of learning are simply compared, stock by stock.
  • pooled: one model for all stocks, blind to which stock a row is
  • pooled + stock: one model that also reads the stock as a category, so a tree can split on a stock wherever enough of its rows say it behaves differently (the in-between)
  • per stock: one model per stock, learned from that stock's rows alone
Every model is the same kind of small boosted tree, and each picks its own leaf size and number of rounds on its own held-out weeks, so none runs on settings sized for another. The measure is the within-stock AUC on VALIDATION: for one stock, how often the model rates a day that turned out positive above a day that did not. 0.5: it cannot tell them apart; 1.0: it always can. It is read inside each stock, so knowing that one stock moves more than another earns nothing; only telling a stock's own days apart counts. Two targets, at 13:30 for the move to 15:30 (the Hurdle and Movers question):
  • moved: did the stock move at least THETA percent, either way?
  • up: did it go up? Every day counts, no threshold

Settings

  1. The question: when the prediction is made, how far ahead, what counts as "moved"
  2. The stocks and the data: the same 40 active stocks and date ranges as the Hurdle notebook. TEST is never loaded here
  3. The inputs and the models: the Hurdle notebook's input table, and the held-out weeks that choose each model's leaf size and rounds
  4. The planted check: which input carries a planted effect, and how strong it is

The stocks

The Movers / Hurdle screen: every stock with 1-minute bars since UNIVERSE_FROM, read on the TRAIN days only; stocks with gaps or under $1 million traded in the window are dropped, and the UNIVERSE_N that most often moved UNIVERSE_THETA percent stay (Table 1).

1 · Head to head

Each approach learns each target on TRAIN, then rates every VALIDATION stock-day. Table 5 gives, per target and approach, the within-stock AUC averaged over the stocks, its median, and on how many stocks the approach is the best of the three. Figure 1 puts every stock on one dot: across, its AUC from the pooled model; up, from the per-stock model (and from pooled + stock). A dot above the grey line is a stock where that approach beats the pooled model. About a minute per target.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Transfer: does a stock's own model know it best?

Every per-stock model rates the VALIDATION days of every stock. Figure 2 (one map per target): a row is the stock whose model is used, a column the stock it rates; blue is better than guessing (AUC above 0.5), red worse. The diagonal is each stock's own model on its own days.
  • If the stocks are different, the diagonal stands out: a stock's own model is the best one for it, and the other stocks' models do worse there
  • If they share their patterns, the diagonal does not stand out: other stocks' models rate a stock about as well as its own, which is what a pooled model uses
Table 7 puts it in numbers per stock: its own model, the average of the other stocks' models on its days, and the pooled model.

data.text/markdown:
3 · The planted check: what each answer looks like

The same real stocks, days and inputs, with planted labels in place of the real ones, so the right answer is known. The labels follow the input PLANT_INPUT (standardized inside each stock) with strength PLANT_STRENGTH, at the real "moved" share:
  • none: the labels ignore every input. All three approaches should sit near 0.5; the spread of the per-stock AUCs over the stocks shows how far apart two numbers land when there is nothing to find
  • shared: every stock follows the input the same way. Pooling should win: the same pattern, learned from all stocks' rows
  • per stock: half of the stocks follow the input, the other half the opposite way. The blind pooled model should lose (the halves cancel, unless other inputs tell them apart); per stock and pooled + stock should find it, and the transfer diagonal should stand out
If the real targets in sections 1 and 2 look like the shared row, one model for all stocks is the better focus; if they look like the per stock row, models per stock are. About three minutes.

data.text/markdown:
Reading the answer

Per target, set sections 1 and 2 beside the planted rows of Table 8:
  • One model for all stocks: pooled is as good as or better than per stock on most stocks, pooled + stock adds nothing, and the transfer diagonal does not stand out. The stocks share what is learnable; one model sees all of it
  • One model per stock: per stock (and pooled + stock) clearly above pooled on most stocks, and each stock's own model beats the other stocks' models on its days
  • In between: pooled + stock the best of the three. Shared patterns plus stock-specific adjustments: keep one model and let it read the stock
  • Nothing either way: all three near 0.5, like the planted "none" row. For that target there is nothing to pool or to split; the choice does not matter until an input that knows something comes along
The per-stock models learn from a few hundred rows each, the pooled ones from all of them: the planted "shared" row shows what that difference costs when the stocks really are alike.
